Human Flourishing
HYOO-mun FLUR-ish-ing
noun phrase
An English rendering of the classical Greek eudaimonia (Aristotle's 'living well,' the good life), revived in modern ethics, positive psychology, and a great deal of recent evangelical writing. Good when it names the full, God-centered well-being of the image-bearer; corrupted when it shrinks into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation cut loose from holiness.

Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
Good when God-centered and holiness-rooted (Ps. 1:2-3), but weaponized into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation severed from holiness.

Biblical Definition

Scripture does have a vision of human well-being — but it is God-centered, holiness-bounded, and oriented to eternity. Christ came 'that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly' (John 10:10), and the abundant life is fellowship with God: 'in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore' (Ps. 16:11). True flourishing is the blessedness of the man whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; he 'shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season' (Ps. 1:2-3) — a flourishing rooted in righteousness, not severed from it. Even the welfare of the city is sought under God: 'seek the peace of the city... for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace' (Jer. 29:7). And the whole of it is ordered to a chief end beyond this life: 'to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.' Man flourishes when he is what he was made to be — God's image-bearer, reconciled, holy, and glad in his Maker — not when he is merely comfortable, affirmed, or self-fulfilled.

Era

A eudaimonia term, good when God-centered (Jer. 29:7; the abundant life of John 10:10), but weaponized into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation severed from holiness and eternity.

HUMAN FLOURISHING, noun phrase. The full well-being or 'living well' of the human being.

An English rendering of Aristotle's eudaimonia, revived in modern ethics and recent evangelical writing.

Sound sense: the God-centered, holiness-rooted blessedness of the image-bearer — the abundant life (John 10:10), fulness of joy in God's presence (Ps. 16:11).

Corrupt drift: shrunk to this-worldly self-actualization, comfort, and affirmation, cut loose from holiness, repentance, and eternity.

Key Scripture

John 10:10 — "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."

Jeremiah 29:7 — "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."

Psalm 1:2-3 — "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper."

Psalm 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Matthew 16:26 — "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?"

Modern Corruption

A good idea — the full well-being of the image-bearer — is shrunk into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation cut loose from holiness, so that 'flourishing' comes to mean comfort and self-fulfillment apart from God.

expand to see more

The corruption is the horizontal collapse of a vertical idea. Biblical flourishing is the blessedness of a creature rightly related to his Creator — the tree planted by the water because its 'delight is in the law of the LORD' (Ps. 1:2-3), the fulness of joy found 'in thy presence' (Ps. 16:11). Cut the root and keep the foliage, and 'human flourishing' becomes a purely this-worldly project: psychological well-being, self-actualization, the realization of one's 'authentic self,' material and emotional thriving measured with no reference to God or to holiness. In much progressive and therapeutic usage the word is then bent further, so that 'flourishing' requires the affirmation of whatever a person desires to be — including the very sins Scripture names — and to call any desire to repentance is recast as an obstacle to someone's 'flourishing.' # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the affirmation-as-flourishing framing is named here to rebut it.

Once severed from holiness, the term inverts the gospel's own calculus. Christ asked, 'what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?' (Matt. 16:26), and called His followers to deny themselves and take up a cross (Matt. 16:24) — a summons that the self-actualization version of 'flourishing' cannot comprehend, for it counts the cross as the opposite of thriving. But the man who 'will save his life shall lose it' (Matt. 16:25). A 'flourishing' that crowns the unsurrendered self, affirms it in its sins, and seeks its best life now is not the abundant life Christ gives but the thief's counterfeit (John 10:10) — a fullness that is empty, because it has gained the world and forfeited the soul.

The recovery is to restore the God-centered, holiness-rooted, eternity-bound vision the word once carried. Yes, seek the welfare of the city and your neighbor's good (Jer. 29:7); yes, the abundant life is real and glad (John 10:10). But man flourishes only as what he was made to be — God's image-bearer, redeemed by Christ, growing in holiness, and finding his joy in God Himself. The chief end of man, and so his deepest flourishing, is 'to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.' True flourishing and holiness are not rivals; the tree flourishes because it is planted by the river of God's law (Ps. 1:3). Sever the holiness and you have not freed flourishing; you have killed the tree and kept the leaves.

Hebrew Roots

A eudaimonia term, sound when God-centered (Ps. 1:2-3; John 10:10), corrupted into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation severed from holiness. Recover the flourishing of the image-bearer rooted in righteousness and oriented to eternity.

expand to see more

Greek: eudaimonia, 'living well,' the good life — Aristotle's term, revived in modern ethics and evangelical writing.

Biblical flourishing: Ps. 1:2-3, the tree by the river whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; John 10:10, the abundant life.

The inversion it forgets: Matt. 16:25-26, save your life and lose it; gain the world and lose the soul — flourishing severed from holiness is the thief's counterfeit.

Usage

"They called repentance an obstacle to her 'flourishing,' but Christ asked what a man profits if he gains the world and loses his soul."

"Cut the root and keep the leaves, and 'human flourishing' shrinks to self-actualization — comfort crowned, holiness forgotten."

"The tree flourishes because it is planted by the river of God's law; sever the holiness and you have killed the tree, not freed it."
